APPLICABLE RULE
49 CFR § 395.3(a) — "Maximum driving time for property-carrying vehicles." This applies to a driver of a property-carrying commercial motor vehicle (CMV) operating in interstate commerce. Passenger-carrying rules (§ 395.5) and the 60/70-hour on-duty limits (§ 395.3(b)) are separate and are not the subject of these three questions.

ANSWERS, WITH THE CONTROLLING TEXT

1) Consecutive hours off duty required before driving: 10 hours.
   § 395.3(a)(1): "A driver may not drive without first taking 10 consecutive hours off duty."
   The 10 hours must be consecutive and must be off duty (or in a sleeper berth, or a qualifying combination, where § 395.1(g) split-sleeper-berth applies). It is a precondition to driving, not merely a pause: the driver cannot drive at all until it is satisfied.

2) Consecutive hours after which the driver may no longer drive: 14 hours.
   § 395.3(a)(2): "A driver may not drive after a period of 14 consecutive hours after coming on-duty following 10 consecutive hours off-duty."
   The 14-hour clock starts when the driver comes on duty following the 10-hour break. Two points worth stating precisely, because the ask's phrasing ("consecutive hours on duty") can be misread:
   - The 14 hours is elapsed clock time from the moment of coming on duty, not accumulated on-duty time. Off-duty time taken inside the window does not pause or extend it.
   - Driving is prohibited after the 14th hour; the driver may still perform non-driving on-duty work after that point (subject to the separate 60/70-hour limits), but may not drive.
   The window is not extendable except by specific regulatory exception — e.g., § 395.3(b)(1) adverse driving conditions (up to 2 additional hours, and only where the driver could not have known of the conditions), or § 395.1(g) sleeper-berth splitting. None is assumed here.

3) Total hours that may be driven within that period: 11 hours.
   § 395.3(a)(3)(i): "A driver may drive a total of 11 hours during the period specified in paragraph (a)(2) of this section."
   The 11 hours is a cumulative cap on driving time inside the 14-hour window. Because 11 < 14, both limits can be simultaneously binding: a driver who drives 11 hours early in the window is barred by the 11-hour rule, and a driver who idles away time is barred at hour 14 with fewer than 11 driving hours.

ADJACENT REQUIREMENT THAT MUST NOT BE CONFUSED WITH THE THREE VALUES
§ 395.3(a)(3)(ii): a driver may not drive after 8 cumulative hours of driving time without at least a 30-minute interruption of driving status (on-duty not driving, off-duty, or sleeper berth). This is a fourth, independent constraint. It does not change the 10-, 14-, or 11-hour figures and is not counted as an answer above, but a compliance determination that applies only the three numbers will be wrong.

WHAT IS DELIBERATELY EXCLUDED
- § 395.3(b): the 60-hour/7-day and 70-hour/8-day on-duty limits. Separate from the three asks; a driver may be within all three limits above and still be out of hours under (b).
- § 395.1(e) short-haul exception: if it applied, the driver would not be subject to § 395.3(a) at all. Not assumed.
- § 395.3(b)(1) adverse driving conditions: an extension, not a baseline value. Not assumed.
- State or carrier policies, which may be stricter but cannot be more permissive.

SUMMARY TABLE
| Constraint | Value | Citation |
|---|---|---|
| Off duty before driving | 10 consecutive hours | § 395.3(a)(1) |
| On-duty window before driving is barred | 14 consecutive hours after coming on duty | § 395.3(a)(2) |
| Driving time within the window | 11 hours total | § 395.3(a)(3)(i) |
| (Not asked) driving-status interruption | 30 minutes after 8 cumulative driving hours | § 395.3(a)(3)(ii) |

SOURCES
49 CFR § 395.3 as published at eCFR (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-49/chapter-III/subchapter-B/part-395/section-395.3) and the GovInfo CFR volumes (CFR-2022-title49-vol5 and CFR-2025-title49-vol5, sec395-3.pdf); the three operative sentences are quoted verbatim above from the eCFR text fetched 2026-11-15.

ANSWERS UNDER 47 CFR § 97.313 (FCC amateur radio service)

| Ask | Limit | Value | Unit | Measure | Rule |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | General maximum transmitter power | 1.5 | kW | PEP (peak envelope power) — i.e. 1500 W PEP | § 97.313(b) |
| 2 | Lower limit on the 10.10–10.15 MHz segment (30 m band) | 200 | W | PEP (peak envelope power) — i.e. 0.2 kW PEP | § 97.313(c)(1) |

Ask 3 ("give each with its unit and measure") is satisfied by the Unit and Measure columns above: both figures are peak envelope power, not average power, not carrier power, and not ERP/EIRP.

1. GENERAL MAXIMUM — 1.5 kW PEP
Governing text, 47 CFR § 97.313(b): "No station may transmit with a transmitter power exceeding 1.5 kW PEP."
- Value: 1.5 kilowatts = 1500 watts.
- Measure: peak envelope power, the average power supplied to the antenna transmission line by a transmitter during one RF cycle at the crest of the modulation envelope under normal operating conditions (definition of PEP in 47 CFR § 97.3, Definitions).
- Scope: this is the ceiling that applies generally, i.e. it is the number a station defaults to on any band where no tighter band-specific limit in § 97.313 applies. It is not license-class dependent and not mode dependent on its face; it is stated as "No station may transmit..." so it binds every amateur station holding privileges on the band in question.
- Practitioner point: 1.5 kW PEP is the ceiling, not an entitlement on every band. Where a subsection of § 97.313 sets a lower figure for a specific band or segment, that lower figure controls.

2. LOWER LIMIT ON 10.10–10.15 MHz — 200 W PEP
Governing text, 47 CFR § 97.313(c): "No station may transmit with a transmitter power output exceeding 200 W PEP: (1) On the 10.10-10.15 MHz segment; ..."
- Value: 200 watts = 0.2 kilowatts.
- Measure: peak envelope power. Note the wording difference — subsection (b) limits "transmitter power" while subsection (c) limits "transmitter power output" (RF power delivered to the antenna transmission line) — but both are quantified in PEP, so the operative measure is the same and the two numbers are directly comparable.
- Scope: applies to all stations, regardless of license class, that hold privileges on 10.10–10.15 MHz (the 30 m band). There is no higher-power carve-out for higher license classes on this segment; the 200 W PEP figure is the maximum, and the general 1.5 kW PEP ceiling may not be used there.
- Relationship to ask 1: 200 W PEP is a strict subset of the 1.5 kW PEP ceiling (200 W < 1500 W). The two figures are not alternatives and must not be conflated: on 10.10–10.15 MHz the answer is 200 W PEP; on bands without a tighter § 97.313 limit the answer is 1.5 kW PEP.

(c) No station may transmit with a transmitter power output exceeding 200 W PEP:
(1) On the 10.10-10.15 MHz segment;"

Part 97 is amended from time to time, and § 97.313 has been amended before. The figures above are stated as of the eCFR text fetched on 2026-11-15. Before relying on them in a licensing, enforcement or equipment-design context, re-verify against the then-current eCFR text and check the FCC's recent rulemaking (e.g. any Report and Order affecting § 97.313) for amendments effective after that date. If the applicable text has changed, the changed figure controls over this answer.

- The separate minimum-power provision in § 97.313(a) (stations must use the minimum power necessary to carry out the desired communications) is a duty, not a maximum, and is deliberately not used here as either of the two requested values.

Those do not change the 200 W PEP figure but do constrain operation; they are context only and are not part of the answer to asks 1 or 2.

ANSWER

Ask 1 — Trigger height. Under 29 CFR § 1926.501(b)(1), an employee on a walking/working surface (horizontal or vertical) with an unprotected side or edge must be protected from falling when that side or edge is 6 feet (1.8 m) or more above a lower level.

Ask 2 — Permitted systems. Protection under that paragraph is provided "by the use of guardrail systems, safety net systems, or personal fall arrest systems." The list is disjunctive ("or"): the employer may select any one of the three, provided the selected system is installed and used in accordance with the applicable criteria. A combination of systems is also acceptable in practice where each component meets its own criteria, though the paragraph itself names the three alternatives rather than combinations.

VERBATIM REGULATORY TEXT RELIED ON

"(1) Unprotected sides and edges. Each employee on a walking/working surface (horizontal and vertical surface) with an unprotected side or edge which is 6 feet (1.8 m) or more above a lower level shall be protected from falling by the use of guardrail systems, safety net systems, or personal fall arrest systems."

— 29 CFR § 1926.501(b)(1), U.S. Code of Federal Regulations, Title 29, Subtitle B, Chapter XVII, Part 1926, Subpart M. Passage retrieved from https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-XVII/part-1926/subpart-M/section-1926.501 (fetched 2026-11-15T09:37:13Z; sha256 3e4c6b147793...). This is a direct quotation from the fetched page, not a paraphrase from memory.

PLAIN-LANGUAGE RESTATEMENT (for training or briefing use)

If a worker can walk or work on a surface and there is an edge with no guardrail or wall protecting it, and the drop from that edge to the surface below is 6 feet (1.8 m) or more, the employer must provide fall protection. The employer chooses the means: a guardrail system, a safety net system, or a personal fall arrest system.

KEY POINTS OF CONSTRUCTION

1. "6 feet (1.8 m) or more" is the threshold. At exactly 6 feet the duty attaches; below 6 feet this paragraph does not impose the duty (other hazards or other standards may still apply).
2. "Walking/working surface" is expressly defined in the paragraph's own parenthetical as a horizontal and vertical surface, so the duty is not limited to floors and roofs.
3. The duty is triggered by an "unprotected" side or edge — i.e., one lacking the protection the standard contemplates. Whether a given wall or barrier counts as protection is a § 1926.500(b) definitional question (see Scope limits below).
4. The obligation runs to the employer; it is a duty to have protection in place, distinct from the separate duty to train employees (§ 1926.503) and from the duty to enforce use.

SCOPE LIMITS — WHAT THIS QUOTE DOES NOT ESTABLISH

The following are outside the verified sentence and are flagged so no one treats them as certified by this answer. Each should be confirmed against the current eCFR before being written into a site procedure, citation, or training slide.

- System design and performance criteria. § 1926.501(b)(1) names the systems; it does not state how they must be built. Those criteria live elsewhere in Subpart M (notably § 1926.502 for guardrail, safety net, personal fall arrest, positioning device, warning line, safety monitoring, and fall protection plan requirements, and § 1926.503 for training). Naming a system here is not a certification that a particular installation complies.
- Other paragraphs of § 1926.501(b). Subpart M sets different or additional triggers for specific conditions — for example leading edges, hoist areas, holes, formwork and reinforcing steel, ramps/runways/walkways, excavations, dangerous equipment, overhand bricklaying, low-slope roofing, steep roofs, pre-cast concrete erection, residential construction, and wall openings. Several of these carry their own height thresholds or their own permitted system sets, and some permit a fall protection plan in lieu of conventional systems where the employer can demonstrate infeasibility. Where one of those paragraphs applies to the task, it governs over the general rule in (b)(1). Paragraph lettering and the exact text of each should be confirmed against the current eCFR before citation.
- § 1926.500(a) scope and § 1926.500(b) definitions. Terms including "lower levels," "unprotected sides and edges," "walking/working surface," and the named systems are defined or scoped in § 1926.500. Those definitions control edge cases (what counts as a lower level; whether an existing wall or parapet is adequate protection). I have not quoted them here and they must be read directly.
- Jurisdiction. This is the federal OSHA construction standard (29 CFR Part 1926). OSHA-approved State Plans must be at least as effective as the federal standard but may differ in threshold or detail; if the work is in a State Plan jurisdiction, the state standard controls. Verify before relying on the 6-foot figure there.
- Industry sector. Part 1926 governs construction. General-industry walking-working surfaces are regulated under 29 CFR Part 1910 and carry a different threshold; that figure is not the answer to this question and is not stated here as a specification.
- Currency of text. The quotation is from the eCFR "current" view as of the fetch timestamp above. Confirm the edition in force on the date of use, and check for any recent amendments, before citing in an enforcement or training document.

# 40 CFR § 50.19 — Ozone NAAQS: level and site-level attainment test

## 1. Direct answer

### 1.1 Level of the standard — § 50.19(a)

The level of the national 8-hour **primary** ambient air quality standard for ozone is **0.070 parts per million (ppm)** (equivalently **70 ppb**), as a **daily maximum 8-hour average**.

Verbatim, 40 CFR § 50.19(a):

> "(a) The level of the national 8-hour primary ambient air quality standard for ozone (O3) is 0.070 parts per million (ppm), daily maximum 8-hour average, measured by a reference method based on appendix D to this part and designated in accordance with part 53 of this chapter or an equivalent method designated in accordance with part 53 of this chapter."

Three components are packed into that one sentence and all three matter operationally:

1. **Numerical level:** 0.070 ppm. Not 0.075 ppm (the superseded 2008 level) and not 0.08 ppm / 0.12 ppm (the superseded 1997 standards).
2. **Averaging time / form of the measurement:** daily maximum 8-hour average. The 8-hour averages are computed from hourly ozone data in accordance with appendix D to part 50; the daily maximum is the highest of that day's valid 8-hour averages. Per appendix D, an 8-hour average is associated with the calendar day on which the 8-hour period begins.
3. **Measurement method:** a reference method based on appendix D and designated under part 53, or an equivalent method designated under part 53. Data from non-designated monitors (e.g., some non-regulatory or special-purpose monitors) do not carry the same regulatory weight.

For completeness: the **secondary** 8-hour ozone standard is also 0.070 ppm (§ 50.19(c)), and it is met by the identical site-level test (§ 50.19(d)). The primary and secondary ozone standards therefore share level and form; they differ only in legal consequence.

### 1.2 When the standard is met at a monitoring site — § 50.19(b)

The standard is **met** at an ambient air quality monitoring site when the **3-year average of the annual fourth-highest daily maximum 8-hour average ozone concentration is less than or equal to 0.070 ppm**, as determined in accordance with appendix U to part 50.

Verbatim, 40 CFR § 50.19(b):

> "(b) The 8-hour primary O3 ambient air quality standard is met at an ambient air quality monitoring site when the 3-year average of the annual fourth-highest daily maximum 8-hour average O3 concentration is less than or equal to 0.070 ppm, as determined in accordance with appendix U to this part."

That quantity — the 3-year average of annual fourth-highest daily maximum 8-hour averages — is the **design value** for the site. The comparison is `design value ≤ 0.070 ppm` → met; `design value > 0.070 ppm` → not met. The test is `≤`, so a design value of exactly 0.070 ppm **meets** the standard; there is no strict-inequality reading and no margin below the level.

## 2. Why the answer is the 0.070 ppm version and not 0.075 ppm

§ 50.19 has carried different numbers across revisions, and the number in the section is only correct relative to a revision:

| Rule / revision | Level (primary, 8-hr) | Form |
|---|---|---|
| 1997 8-hour ozone NAAQS | 0.08 ppm | 3-yr avg of annual 4th-highest daily max 8-hr avg |
| 2008 8-hour ozone NAAQS | 0.075 ppm | same form |
| **2015 8-hour ozone NAAQS (current codified § 50.19)** | **0.070 ppm** | **same form** |

EPA's subsequent review retained the 0.070 ppm level; the codified text of § 50.19(a) as currently published is 0.070 ppm, and that is the figure this answer states. Any future revision of the ozone NAAQS would change § 50.19(a) and this answer with it — the number is revision-dependent, not a permanent constant. If the requester needed the 2008 rule (e.g., for a historical designation or a state implementation plan obligation tied to the 2008 standard), the correct value would be 0.075 ppm; that is a different question and is flagged here only so the 0.070 ppm figure is not misapplied to a 2008-standard obligation.

## 3. How the design value is built — the four-step computation

Given a monitor's quality-assured hourly ozone record:

1. **Hourly → 8-hour averages.** Compute 8-hour averages from the hourly values per appendix D; assign each 8-hour average to the calendar day on which its 8-hour period begins.
2. **Daily → daily maximum 8-hour average.** For each day with sufficient valid 8-hour averages, take the maximum. That single number is the day's value; the other 8-hour averages that day are discarded for NAAQS purposes.
3. **Annual → fourth-highest.** Rank each calendar year's daily maximum 8-hour averages and take the **fourth-highest** (not the highest, not the 98th percentile). A year with three or fewer valid daily maxima still has a fourth-highest value only if it has at least four; otherwise that year cannot supply a fourth-highest and the design value cannot be formed from it as-is (see § 4.2).
4. **Three years → design value.** Average the annual fourth-highest values for three consecutive years: `DV = (4th-high_yr1 + 4th-high_yr2 + 4th-high_yr3) / 3`. Round per appendix U, then compare to 0.070 ppm.

Note what this form does and does not do. It is deliberately insensitive to a single extreme day (the highest value is dropped) but it is not a percentile-of-days statistic and it is not an annual-mean statistic: one bad year out of three can carry a site over the level, and three years are required so that year-to-year meteorology is partly averaged out.

## 4. Operational conventions from appendix U that decide close cases

§ 50.19(b) incorporates appendix U by reference ("as determined in accordance with appendix U"), so the appendix, not the one-line section text, resolves the borderline cases. The appendix text governs where the two could be read differently; the points below are the ones that change outcomes.

### 4.1 Rounding before comparison

The design value is rounded to **three decimal places (nearest 0.001 ppm, i.e. nearest 1 ppb)** before it is compared to 0.070 ppm. This is not cosmetic. Because the annual fourth-highest values are effectively whole ppb, a 3-year average lands on thirds of a ppb, and the rounding step decides the outcome:

- `(70 + 70 + 71) / 3 = 70.333 ppb = 0.070333 ppm` → rounds to **0.070** → **met**.
- `(70 + 71 + 71) / 3 = 70.667 ppb = 0.070667 ppm` → rounds to **0.071** → **not met**.

The first line is the one that looks wrong if the rounding convention is ignored: 0.070333 is numerically greater than 0.070, yet the site meets the standard because the rounded design value is 0.070. Applying the rounding step is mandatory, not a convenience.

### 4.2 Data completeness

A year's data must be sufficiently complete before its fourth-highest value can be used: at least **75 percent** of the scheduled sampling days in the year must have valid daily maximum 8-hour averages, and a given day's maximum must itself be supported by a sufficient share of that day's possible 8-hour averages (75 percent of the 8-hour periods). Years that fail completeness are handled under appendix U's provisions — which address when a design value may be computed from fewer than three complete years, and what happens when a monitor's record is short (e.g., a newly established monitor) or when one year in the three-year window is incomplete. The appendix controls the specific mechanics; the practitioner should read appendix U directly rather than extrapolate from the 75 percent figure alone.

### 4.3 Exceptional events

Air quality data influenced by wildfires, high-wind dust, or other event types that meet the criteria of 40 CFR § 50.14 may be excluded from the regulatory record upon an approved exceptional-events demonstration. Where such data are excluded, they are removed before the design value is computed. This is a separate regulatory track from § 50.19 and appendix U and should not be conflated with a data-completeness adjustment.

### 4.4 Site-specificity

The determination in § 50.19(b) is made **at an ambient air quality monitoring site** — it is a per-site determination. Each monitor has its own design value; two monitors in the same county can and do differ. Area-wide attainment or nonattainment designation is a separate step under Clean Air Act § 107 and 40 CFR part 81, built from the set of site-level design values in the area plus other statutory factors. § 50.19(b) answers "is the standard met at this site?", not "is this area designated attainment?".

## 5. Worked decision procedure and examples

Procedure for a single site with three consecutive years of complete, quality-assured data:

```
for each year y in {y1, y2, y3}:
    a[y] = 4th highest daily maximum 8-hour O3 average in year y   # ppb
DV_raw = (a[y1] + a[y2] + a[y3]) / 3                                # ppb
DV     = round(DV_raw, 3 decimal places in ppm, i.e. nearest 1 ppb)
if DV <= 0.070 ppm:  standard is MET at the site
else:                standard is NOT MET at the site
```

| Case | Annual 4th-highs (ppm) | Unrounded mean | Rounded DV | Verdict vs 0.070 ppm |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | 0.072, 0.069, 0.071 | 0.070667 | 0.071 | **Not met** (0.071 > 0.070) |
| B | 0.070, 0.071, 0.070 | 0.070333 | 0.070 | **Met** (0.070 ≤ 0.070) |
| C | 0.073, 0.073, 0.073 | 0.073000 | 0.073 | **Not met** (0.073 > 0.070) |
| D | 0.068, 0.070, 0.072 | 0.070000 | 0.070 | **Met** (0.070 ≤ 0.070) |

Check on the arithmetic and on consistency with the single 0.070 ppm threshold: A = 0.212/3 = 0.070667 → 0.071 (above, not met); B = 0.211/3 = 0.070333 → 0.070 (at the level, met); C = 0.219/3 = 0.073 (above, not met); D = 0.210/3 = 0.070 exactly (at the level, met). No example labelled "met" exceeds 0.070 after rounding, and no example labelled "not met" is at or below it. Case D is the boundary case worth remembering: a site can sit exactly on the level and still be in attainment, and one year at 0.072 does not by itself defeat a site that is otherwise at 0.070.

## 6. Statement of the answer in one paragraph

Under 40 CFR § 50.19(a), the national 8-hour primary ambient air quality standard for ozone is **0.070 ppm**, daily maximum 8-hour average, measured by an appendix D reference method or a part 53 equivalent method. Under § 50.19(b), that standard is **met at an ambient air quality monitoring site when the 3-year average of the annual fourth-highest daily maximum 8-hour average ozone concentration — the design value — is less than or equal to 0.070 ppm**, as determined in accordance with appendix U to part 50, which supplies the rounding (three decimal places) and data-completeness conventions that govern the comparison. The determination is made site by site; it is not itself an area designation.

## 7. Sources

- 40 CFR § 50.19 (current eCFR text), https://ecfr.gov/current/title-40/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-50/section-50.19 — quoted verbatim in § 1 above.
- 40 CFR part 50, appendix U (Interpretation of the 8-Hour Primary and Secondary National Ambient Air Quality Standards for Ozone), http://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-40/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-50/appendix-Appendix%20U%20to%20Part%2050 — controls the design-value computation, rounding, and completeness mechanics.
- 40 CFR part 50, appendix D — 8-hour ozone averaging and daily-maximum conventions.
- 40 CFR § 50.14 — exceptional events.
- 40 CFR part 81 / CAA § 107 — area designations (distinct from the site-level test).

# NIST SP 800-63B-4 — Verifier password length requirements

## 1. Answers

| # | Ask | Value | Normative keyword | Source |
|---|-----|-------|-------------------|--------|
| 1 | Minimum length, password used as a **single-factor** authentication mechanism | **15 characters** | SHALL | SP 800-63B-4, §3.1.1.2 *Password Verifiers* |
| 2 | Minimum length, password used **only as part of multi-factor** authentication | **8 characters** | SHALL (prefaced by MAY-be-shorter) | SP 800-63B-4, §3.1.1.2 *Password Verifiers* |
| 3 | Maximum length verifiers should permit **at least** | **64 characters** | SHOULD (at least) | SP 800-63B-4, §3.1.1.2 *Password Verifiers* |

### Verbatim text (as fetched from the NIST publication PDF)

1. “Verifiers and CSPs SHALL require passwords that are used as a single-factor authentication mechanism to be a minimum of 15 characters in length.”
2. “Verifiers and CSPs MAY allow passwords that are only used as part of multi-factor authentication processes to be shorter but SHALL require them to be a minimum of eight characters in length.”
3. “Verifiers and CSPs SHOULD permit a maximum password length of at least 64 characters.”

Source: NIST SP 800-63B-4, *Digital Identity Guidelines: Authentication and Authenticator Management*, §3.1.1.2 Password Verifiers — https://tsapps.nist.gov/publication/get_pdf.cfm?pub_id=959882 (fetched 2026-11-15T09:39:15Z, sha256 1afebb9b0b7a); also published at https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b/authenticators/.

### Reading the normative keywords correctly

- **15 is a floor, not a target.** It applies whenever the password can authenticate on its own. A verifier that accepts 12 characters for a standalone password is non-conformant.
- **8 is a hard floor too.** The “MAY allow … shorter” clause permits shortening *relative to 15*, but the SHALL in the same sentence pins the absolute minimum at 8. Nothing permits 7.
- **64 is a floor on the verifier's ceiling.** It does not mean “reject passwords longer than 64”; it means the verifier's accepted maximum must be at least 64. A verifier whose max is 32 or 50 is non-conformant. A verifier whose max is 64, 256 or 1024 conforms. The keyword is SHOULD, so it is a recommendation rather than an absolute requirement — but it is free to satisfy, and every major implementation guidance treats it as mandatory in practice. Implement it as mandatory.
- **Consequence for passwords between 8 and 14 characters:** they are acceptable *only* for credentials whose sole use is as one factor among several. If such a password can ever be used alone (see §2.1), the 15-character rule governs.

### Internal consistency check on the three values

- 8 < 15: no conflict; they are alternative minimums selected by usage context, never both applied to the same credential.
- 64 > 15 and 64 > 8: the ceiling floor is strictly above both minimums, so a password at either minimum is also well inside the accepted range.
- The configured hard ceiling in the reference implementation below is **1024 characters**, i.e. 16× the 64 floor — so no code path in this deliverable rejects a password that ask 3 says must be accepted.
- A **63-character** password must still be accepted. The 64 rule bounds the maximum upward, it does not create a 64-character minimum. The test vectors in §6 assert this explicitly, because this is the most common misreading of the requirement.

---

## 2. Backend implementation specification

### 2.1 Step 1 — classify the credential by its *weakest* usage

The length rule is a property of the credential's usage, so the verifier must know at validation time which context applies. Do not infer it from the current request alone; store it.

```
context = SINGLE_FACTOR  if the password can authenticate a session on its own
          MFA_ONLY       otherwise (a second factor is always and unconditionally required)
```

Classification rules, applied in order (first match wins):

| Condition | Context | Min length |
|---|---|---|
| Password is the only factor at login | SINGLE_FACTOR | 15 |
| Password + “remember this device” / long-lived session cookie that bypasses the second factor | SINGLE_FACTOR | 15 |
| Password is accepted for account recovery, self-service reset, or identity proofing on its own | SINGLE_FACTOR | 15 |
| Password can be used with a fallback factor the user can self-enrol (SMS, recovery codes) where the second factor is not enforced server-side | SINGLE_FACTOR | 15 |
| Password is always accompanied by a phishing-resistant or server-enforced second factor (AAL2/AAL3 policy, no bypass) | MFA_ONLY | 8 |
| Context unknown / feature flag unset / ambiguous | SINGLE_FACTOR | 15 |

The last row is the fail-safe default: when in doubt, apply the stricter rule.

**The classification is a stored, versioned property of the credential, not a per-request guess.** If an account is later downgraded to password-only (e.g. an admin disables MFA, or the user loses their second factor and support turns it off), the verifier must force a password change to ≥15 at that moment, because the credential has just become single-factor.

### 2.2 Step 2 — count characters as Unicode code points

NIST counts each Unicode code point as one character when evaluating password length. This is not the same as bytes and not the same as UTF-16 code units.

| Language | Correct | Wrong (undercounts/overcounts astral chars) |
|---|---|---|
| Python | `len(pw)` (str is code points) | `len(pw.encode())` (bytes) |
| JavaScript / TypeScript | `[...pw].length` or `Array.from(pw).length` | `pw.length` (UTF-16 units) |
| Java | `pw.codePointCount(0, pw.length())` | `pw.length()` (UTF-16 units) |
| Go | `utf8.RuneCountInString(pw)` | `len(pw)` (bytes) |
| Rust | `pw.chars().count()` | `pw.len()` (bytes) |

Why it matters concretely: the string `🔐🔐🔐🔐` (four lock emoji) is 4 code points, 8 UTF-16 units, 16 UTF-8 bytes. A Java or JS verifier using the naive length would accept it as an 8-character MFA password when it is really 4 characters — a 2× weakening of the minimum. Conversely a byte-based check would accept `ééé` (3 code points, 6 bytes in UTF-8) as 6 characters.

Do **not** apply Unicode normalization before counting, and do **not** collapse combining sequences into grapheme clusters: `e` + U+0301 (combining acute) is 2 code points and counts as 2.

### 2.3 Step 3 — validation order and what not to do

Order matters for both security and user experience:

1. Reject empty / missing input.
2. **Length check** (this document).
3. Blocklist check (common/breached passwords) — NIST requires a blocklist; it is out of scope for the three values asked but must not be omitted from the pipeline.
4. Rate-limit / lockout accounting.
5. Hash and store.

Explicit prohibitions that interact with the length rules:

- **Never truncate.** Not to 64, not to 72 (bcrypt), not to any column width. Truncation makes distinct secrets equivalent and silently defeats the length policy. If input exceeds the ceiling, *reject* it; do not shorten it.
- **Never trim whitespace.** Leading and trailing spaces are part of the secret and count toward length. Guard against accidental trimming in HTML forms, JSON decoders, and middleware.
- **Do not impose composition rules** (mixed case / digit / symbol requirements) alongside the length rule; they push users toward shorter, more predictable passwords. This is separate guidance, not one of the three asks, but it is the usual source of a length policy being quietly undermined.
- **Do not cap below 64.** Any configurable maximum must be validated at startup to be ≥ 64, and the service should refuse to boot otherwise.

### 2.4 Reference implementation (Python)

```python
# password_policy.py — NIST SP 800-63B-4 §3.1.1.2 length rules
from __future__ import annotations

import base64
import hashlib
from dataclasses import dataclass
from enum import Enum

SINGLE_FACTOR_MIN_CHARS = 15      # SHALL
MFA_ONLY_MIN_CHARS = 8            # SHALL (floor, even though MAY be shorter than 15)
MIN_ACCEPTED_MAX_CHARS = 64       # SHOULD: verifier's ceiling must be >= this
HARD_CEILING_CHARS = 1024         # local DoS bound; invariant: >= MIN_ACCEPTED_MAX_CHARS

assert HARD_CEILING_CHARS >= MIN_ACCEPTED_MAX_CHARS, "ceiling would violate the 64-character floor"


class Context(str, Enum):
    SINGLE_FACTOR = "single_factor"
    MFA_ONLY = "mfa_only"


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class PolicyError:
    code: str
    message: str
    required_min: int | None = None
    configured_max: int | None = None


def char_length(password: str) -> int:
    """Unicode code points, per NIST counting rule."""
    return len(password)  # Python str indexes code points, not bytes or UTF-16 units


def min_length_for(ctx: Context) -> int:
    return MFA_ONLY_MIN_CHARS if ctx is Context.MFA_ONLY else SINGLE_FACTOR_MIN_CHARS


def validate_length(password: str, ctx: Context) -> PolicyError | None:
    n = char_length(password)
    minimum = min_length_for(ctx)
    if n < minimum:
        return PolicyError(
            code="password_too_short",
            message=f"Password must be at least {minimum} characters.",
            required_min=minimum,
        )
    if n > HARD_CEILING_CHARS:
        # Reject, never truncate.
        return PolicyError(
            code="password_too_long",
            message=f"Password must be at most {HARD_CEILING_CHARS} characters.",
            configured_max=HARD_CEILING_CHARS,
        )
    return None


def hash_for_storage(password: str) -> bytes:
    """Argon2id preferred: no input truncation at any length."""
    from argon2.low_level import hash_secret_raw, Type
    return hash_secret_raw(
        secret=password.encode("utf-8"),
        salt=__import__("os").urandom(16),
        time_cost=3, memory_cost=65536, parallelism=4,
        hash_len=32, type=Type.ID,
    )


def bcrypt_input(password: str) -> bytes:
    """If bcrypt is unavoidable: bcrypt silently ignores bytes past 72.
    Pre-hash so that 64-character (and longer, multi-byte) passwords remain
    fully significant and two distinct long passwords cannot collide."""
    return base64.b64encode(hashlib.sha256(password.encode("utf-8")).digest())
```

### 2.5 Equivalent length check in other runtimes

```typescript
// TypeScript
const SINGLE_FACTOR_MIN = 15;
const MFA_ONLY_MIN = 8;
const HARD_CEILING = 1024; // must be >= 64

export function charLength(pw: string): number {
  return [...pw].length; // code points, NOT pw.length (UTF-16 units)
}

export function validateLength(
  pw: string,
  ctx: 'single_factor' | 'mfa_only',
): { ok: true } | { ok: false; code: string; min?: number; max?: number } {
  const n = charLength(pw);
  const min = ctx === 'mfa_only' ? MFA_ONLY_MIN : SINGLE_FACTOR_MIN;
  if (n < min) return { ok: false, code: 'password_too_short', min };
  if (n > HARD_CEILING) return { ok: false, code: 'password_too_long', max: HARD_CEILING };
  return { ok: true };
}
```

```java
// Java
public static final int SINGLE_FACTOR_MIN = 15;
public static final int MFA_ONLY_MIN = 8;
public static final int HARD_CEILING = 1024; // >= 64

public static int charLength(String pw) {
    return pw.codePointCount(0, pw.length()); // not pw.length()
}
```

### 2.6 Storage schema

```sql
CREATE TABLE credentials (
    user_id              UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    password_hash        BYTEA       NOT NULL,           -- Argon2id output; never plaintext
    hash_algorithm       TEXT        NOT NULL,           -- 'argon2id-v1', 'bcrypt-sha256-v1'
    password_context     TEXT        NOT NULL            -- drives the minimum length
        CHECK (password_context IN ('single_factor', 'mfa_only')),
    password_char_length INTEGER     NOT NULL            -- code points, for policy audit only
        CHECK (password_char_length >= 1 AND password_char_length <= 1024),
    policy_version       TEXT        NOT NULL,           -- e.g. 'sp800-63b-4'
    changed_at           TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    must_change_at_login BOOLEAN     NOT NULL DEFAULT false
);

-- Invariant enforced at the application layer on write:
--   password_context = 'single_factor'  => password_char_length >= 15
--   password_context = 'mfa_only'       => password_char_length >= 8
-- There is no upper CHECK at 64: the ceiling is 1024, and 64 is a floor on that ceiling.
```

Do not store the plaintext or a reversible form. `password_char_length` is metadata for policy auditing and for driving the “upgrade on next login” flow; it is not a secret.

### 2.7 API error contract

```json
{
  "error": "password_too_short",
  "message": "Password must be at least 15 characters.",
  "required_min_characters": 15
}
```

- Return HTTP 422 for policy rejections.
- Publishing the length policy in the error is fine and helpful — the policy is public.
- Do **not** distinguish “found in blocklist” from other rejections in a way that reveals blocklist membership or lets an attacker probe it; use a generic message for that case and keep the response timing uniform.
- The minimum returned must be the context-specific one (15 or 8), never a single global constant, so that clients render correct guidance.

---

## 3. Interaction with other verifier requirements

These are not among the three asks but are the things most likely to invalidate a correct length implementation:

1. **Blocklist.** A password that meets the length rule can still be rejected. Apply both; the length rule is necessary, not sufficient. In particular, `12345678` is exactly 8 characters and satisfies the MFA floor on length while being worthless.
2. **Character acceptance.** Verifiers must accept all printable ASCII including space, and Unicode; combined with code-point counting this is what makes the 64-character floor meaningful for non-Latin scripts.
3. **No composition rules.** Do not add “must contain a symbol” on top of the length rule.
4. **No periodic forced rotation.** Rotation drives users to predictable increments and undermines the entropy the longer minimum is buying. Force change only on compromise or on a context downgrade.
5. **DoS bound.** The 1024-character ceiling exists so that an attacker cannot force unbounded hashing work. It is far above the 64-character floor, so it does not conflict with ask 3. If using bcrypt, remember its 72-**byte** truncation: a 64-character password in a 3-byte-per-character script is 192 bytes and would be silently truncated — pre-hash as shown in §2.4 or use Argon2id.

---

## 4. Migration and grandfathering

Existing credentials may be shorter than the new minimums. The safe rollout:

1. Do **not** lock anyone out at login. Authenticate normally, then, on successful authentication, if `password_char_length < min_length_for(password_context)`, set `must_change_at_login = true`.
2. On the forced change, enforce the correct minimum for the credential's context.
3. Reclassify every credential whose context is ambiguous to `single_factor` and force the 15-character upgrade.
4. Time-box the grandfathering window (e.g. 90 days) and report the count of un-upgraded credentials as a compliance metric. Accepting a 10-character single-factor password indefinitely is a standing deviation from the SHALL, and should be tracked as such rather than quietly tolerated.
5. Never “upgrade” by truncating, padding, or re-hashing the old password at a new length — the user must choose a new secret.

---

## 5. Acceptance tests

| # | Input | Code points | Context | Expected | Why |
|---|-------|-------------|---------|----------|-----|
| 1 | `correcthorsebat` | 14 | single_factor | reject, `password_too_short`, min 15 | just below ask 1 |
| 2 | `correcthorsebatt` | 15 | single_factor | accept (length) | exactly ask 1 |
| 3 | `correcthorsebat` | 14 | mfa_only | accept (length) | above ask 2 |
| 4 | `12345678` | 8 | mfa_only | accept (length), reject (blocklist) | exactly ask 2; proves the two checks are independent |
| 5 | `1234567` | 7 | mfa_only | reject, min 8 | one below ask 2 |
| 6 | `1234567` | 7 | single_factor | reject, min 15 | never 8 for standalone |
| 7 | 64 × `a` | 64 | single_factor | accept | exactly ask 3 |
| 8 | 64 × `a` | 64 | mfa_only | accept | exactly ask 3 |
| 9 | 63 × `a` | 63 | single_factor | accept | ask 3 is a floor on the ceiling, not a 64-char minimum |
| 10 | 200 × `a` | 200 | single_factor | accept | ceiling is 1024, not 64 |
| 11 | 1025 × `a` | 1025 | single_factor | reject, `password_too_long` | local DoS ceiling only |
| 12 | `🔐🔐🔐🔐` | 4 | mfa_only | reject | UTF-16 naive length (8) would wrongly pass |
| 13 | `🔐🔐🔐🔐🔐🔐🔐🔐` | 8 | mfa_only | accept (length) | astral chars count once each |
| 14 | `é` written as `e`+U+0301, ×8 | 16 | single_factor | accept | combining marks are separate code points |
| 15 | `          password` | 18 | single_factor | accept, and hash must include the spaces | no trimming anywhere in the pipeline |
| 16 | 64 × `Ω` (2 bytes each) with bcrypt-sha256 path | 64 | single_factor | accept, and `Ω`-variant passwords must not collide | proves the 72-byte bcrypt truncation is neutralised |

Threshold-adjacent cases (1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 9) are the ones that actually guard the three values; the rest guard the implementation around them.

---

## 6. Caveats and sources

**Revision status.** These values are for SP 800-63B-4. They differ from SP 800-63B-3, which required a minimum of 8 characters for memorized secrets generally and recommended permitting at least 64. Any secondary summary or internal wiki quoting “8 characters” as the single-factor minimum is quoting the superseded revision. Confirm against the final published SP 800-63B-4 text before locking the values into a compliance artifact; if the organisation is still bound to 800-63B-3, the single-factor minimum reverts to 8 and asks 1 and 2 collapse to the same value.

**Normative strength of ask 3.** The fetched passage uses SHOULD, not SHALL. The implementation here treats 64 as a mandatory floor on the verifier's ceiling anyway, because satisfying it has no security cost and because non-conformance is trivially avoidable. If a strict reading is required for an audit artifact, cite it as SHOULD.

**Scope.** “Password” is read as the memorized secret used for authentication, per §3.1.1.2. PINs and other non-password memorized secrets, and password-based key derivation for other purposes, are outside these three values.

**Sources**
- NIST SP 800-63B-4, §3.1.1.2 Password Verifiers — https://tsapps.nist.gov/publication/get_pdf.cfm?pub_id=959882 (fetched 2026-11-15T09:39:15Z, sha256 1afebb9b0b7a)

# Hours-of-service limits for a property-carrying CMV driver — 49 CFR § 395.3(a)

## 1. Scope and authority

- **Rule:** 49 CFR § 395.3, "Maximum driving time for property-carrying vehicles," paragraph (a).
- **Opening text of § 395.3(a)** (verbatim, current eCFR): *"(a) Except as otherwise provided in § 395.1, no motor carrier shall permit or require any driver used by it to drive a property-carrying commercial motor vehicle, nor shall any such driver drive a property-carrying commercial motor vehicle, regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services, unless the driver complies with the following requirements:"*
- **Assumed posture (stated, not hidden):** a standard, non-exempt property-carrying CMV driver; current CFR text; the question asks for the rule itself, not a determination on a particular logbook. If any of those assumptions is wrong, § 4 below identifies what changes.
- **Regulatory posture of the three limits:** they are independent prohibitions, not a menu. The driver must satisfy all three at all times. The carrier is separately prohibited from permitting or requiring a violation, so the limits bind both driver and motor carrier.

## 2. The three answers

| # | Question | Answer | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Consecutive hours off duty required before driving | **10 consecutive hours off duty** | § 395.3(a)(1) |
| 2 | Consecutive hours after coming on duty after which the driver may no longer drive | **14 consecutive hours** after coming on duty following 10 consecutive hours off duty | § 395.3(a)(2) |
| 3 | Total hours that may be driven within that period | **11 hours** of driving following 10 consecutive hours off duty | § 395.3(a)(3)(i) |

Operative content of each paragraph (paraphrased for application; verify wording against the current eCFR text before publishing):

- **(a)(1) — the 10-hour reset.** The driver may not drive until at least 10 consecutive hours off duty have been taken following the end of the prior on-duty period. The 10 hours must be *consecutive*; it may not be assembled from fragments (subject only to the sleeper-berth split discussed in § 4.3).
- **(a)(2) — the 14-hour window.** The driver may not drive after the 14th consecutive hour after coming on duty, following 10 consecutive hours off duty. Off-duty time does not extend or pause the 14-hour period.
- **(a)(3)(i) — the 11-hour driving limit.** The driver may not drive more than 11 hours following 10 consecutive hours off duty. The 11 hours must fall inside the 14-hour window.
- **(a)(3)(ii) — the 30-minute break** (context, not one of the three asks). A driver may not drive if more than 8 *cumulative* hours have passed since the end of the driver's last interruption of at least 30 minutes of driving. The 30 minutes may be satisfied by on-duty-not-driving, off-duty, or sleeper-berth time. It does **not** pause the 14-hour window.

## 3. How the three limits interact (the part that is usually gotten wrong)

1. **The clock starts once.** All three limits are measured from the end of the same 10-hour off-duty period. The 14-hour window and the 11-hour driving allowance both begin running when the driver comes on duty after that reset.
2. **Driving stops at the first limit to expire.** Driving is prohibited at whichever occurs first:
   - the 11th hour of driving, or
   - the 14th hour after coming on duty, or
   - the 8th cumulative hour of driving without a qualifying 30-minute interruption, or
   - exhaustion of the 60-hour/7-day or 70-hour/8-day cumulative on-duty allowance.
3. **The 14-hour window is elapsed time, not on-duty time.** This is the precision point on ask 2. The ask says "consecutive hours on duty"; the rule says *consecutive hours after coming on duty*. A two-hour off-duty lunch inside the shift consumes two hours of the 14-hour window without adding any on-duty time. So the correct statement to a driver is: **you get 14 clock hours from the moment you come on duty, and that clock does not stop.**
4. **Nothing pauses the 14-hour window** — not a meal break, not fueling, not a nap, not a 30-minute break, not detention time at a shipper. Only a qualifying sleeper-berth period (§ 4.3) or the adverse-driving extension (§ 4.1) changes the calculation.
5. **The 10-hour reset restarts everything.** After a full 10 consecutive hours off duty, the driver gets a new 14-hour window and a new 11-hour driving allowance (subject to the cumulative 60/70-hour ceiling).

**Worked example (numbers chosen to satisfy every limit simultaneously).** Driver completes 10 consecutive hours off duty at 06:00 and comes on duty.

| Event | Clock | Driving accumulated | Window remaining |
|---|---|---|---|
| On duty | 06:00 | 0:00 | 14:00 |
| Drive 3:00 | 09:00 | 3:00 | 11:00 |
| On-duty not driving 1:00 (loading) | 10:00 | 3:00 | 10:00 |
| Drive 5:00 | 15:00 | 8:00 | 5:00 |
| 30-min break required here (8 cumulative driving hours reached) | 15:30 | 8:00 | 4:30 |
| Drive 3:00 | 18:30 | 11:00 | 1:30 |
| **Driving prohibited — 11-hour limit reached at 18:30, before the 14-hour window expires at 20:00** | | | |

Had the load taken three hours longer to load, the 14-hour window would have expired at 20:00 and driving would have been prohibited then, with driving hours still unused — the classic "14 beats 11" outcome.

## 4. What would change these three numbers (scope boundaries)

These are the exceptions the opening clause of § 395.3(a) ("Except as otherwise provided in § 395.1") preserves. A real-world answer that omits them is incomplete; none of them applies to the baseline driver assumed above.

1. **Adverse driving conditions — § 395.1(b)(1).** Driving time may be extended by up to **2 hours**, and the 14-hour window is extended by the same amount, when the driver encounters unusually adverse conditions (snow, ice, fog, unusual traffic congestion) that could not reasonably have been known before dispatch. The extension applies to the 11 and the 14, never to the 10-hour reset, and never to the 60/70-hour ceiling.
2. **Short-haul / 150 air-mile operations — § 395.1(e).** The several short-haul paragraphs relieve qualifying drivers of parts of the § 395.3(a) structure (record-of-duty-status requirements and, depending on the paragraph, elements such as the 30-minute break) while still capping the workday. Which specific paragraphs of § 395.3(a) are displaced depends on the subparagraph and on CDL versus non-CDL status, so a short-haul determination must be made paragraph by paragraph against the current text — it cannot be summarized as "10/14/11 does not apply."
3. **Sleeper berth — § 395.1 (sleeper-berth provisions).** A driver may split the required 10-hour off-duty period between a longer sleeper-berth period and a shorter rest period in or out of the berth, with the two totaling at least 10 hours. When a split is validly taken, the qualifying longer sleeper-berth period is excluded from the 14-hour window and the 11-hour driving limit is recalculated from the end of the first qualifying period. This is the one lawful mechanism that effectively pauses the 14-hour window.
4. **Cumulative on-duty limits.** The 60-hour/7-day and 70-hour/8-day ceilings and the 34-hour restart found elsewhere in § 395.3 operate independently and can prohibit driving even when the 10/14/11 limits are all satisfied.
5. **Passenger-carrying vehicles — § 395.5.** Different figures apply (15-hour on-duty window, 10 hours driving, 10 hours off duty). The question correctly scopes to property-carrying; do not reuse 10/14/11 for passenger operations.
6. **State law and intrastate operations.** Some states impose their own intrastate hours-of-service rules that differ from Part 395. Federal limits are a floor only where they apply.
7. **Version currency.** The 10/14/11 core figures have been stable for two decades, but § 395.3(a)(3)(ii) and the sleeper-berth split rules were materially amended by the 2020 hours-of-service rulemaking. Any answer should be pinned to the current eCFR text (§ 395.3, § 395.1) with the retrieval date recorded, because a logbook audited today is judged against the rule in force on the date of the duty status, not the rule in force at audit.

## 5. Plain-language restatement for the driver

> You need **10 consecutive hours off duty** before you can drive again. Once you come on duty, you have a **14-hour window** that starts running and does not stop for breaks, meals, or waiting — you cannot drive after the 14th hour. Inside that window you may drive no more than **11 hours**. You must also take a **30-minute break** from driving after 8 cumulative hours of driving. Driving stops at whichever of those comes first.

## 6. Compliance-check procedure (to apply the rule to a log)

1. Identify the end of the last qualifying 10-consecutive-hour off-duty period (or valid sleeper-berth split). If none exists, no driving is permitted — stop.
2. Mark that point as T0. Compute the 14-hour deadline as T0 + 14:00, adjusted only for a valid adverse-driving extension (up to +2:00) or a valid sleeper-berth split.
3. Sum driving time from T0. The 11-hour driving ceiling is T0-relative, capped independently at 11:00.
4. Walk the log chronologically and flag the earliest of: (a) 11:00 driving; (b) T0 + 14:00; (c) any driving after 8:00 cumulative driving since the last ≥30-minute interruption; (d) exhaustion of the 60/70-hour allowance.
5. Any driving entry timestamped after the flagged point is a violation of § 395.3(a); record which subparagraph was breached, since the citation differs.
6. Confirm no intervening qualifying 10-hour reset or sleeper-berth split resets T0 mid-analysis.

# Transmitter power limits under 47 CFR § 97.313

## 1. Direct answers

| # | Question | Answer | Measure | Governing text |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | General maximum transmitter power for an amateur station | **1.5 kW (1500 W)** | **PEP** — peak envelope power | § 97.313(b) |
| 2 | Lower limit on the 10.10–10.15 MHz segment | **200 W** | **PEP** — peak envelope power | § 97.313(c), introductory text + (c)(1) |

Both figures are stated in the same measure (PEP), so they are directly comparable: 200 W PEP = 0.2 kW PEP, which is 13.3% of the 1.5 kW PEP general ceiling. The 10.10–10.15 MHz figure is therefore a genuine band-specific *reduction* below the general maximum, not an alternative to it.

## 2. Verbatim rule text relied on

- **§ 97.313(b):** "No station may transmit with a transmitter power exceeding 1.5 kW PEP."
  Source: http://ecfr.gov/current/title-47/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-97/subpart-D/section-97.313 (fetched 2026-11-15T09:42:04Z, sha256 1fd41c2c2b71)

- **§ 97.313(c) and (c)(1):** "(c) No station may transmit with a transmitter power output exceeding 200 W PEP: (1) On the 10.10-10.15 MHz segment;"
  Source: same eCFR fetch as above (sha256 1fd41c2c2b71)

- **§ 97.313(a)** (qualifier, not a wattage): "(a) An amateur station must use the minimum transmitter power necessary to carry out the desired communications."
  Source: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2024-title47-vol5/xml/CFR-2024-title47-vol5-part97.xml (fetched 2026-11-15T09:42:04Z, sha256 6b62eb3a3219)

## 3. How the two provisions interact

- § 97.313(b) is the **general ceiling**: it applies to every amateur station and to every band, unless a more specific provision in the same section lowers it.
- § 97.313(c) is a **band-specific ceiling**: its introductory text and subparagraph (1) cap transmitter power output at 200 W PEP on the whole 10.10–10.15 MHz segment (the 30 m band, 10.1–10.15 MHz).
- A station operating anywhere in 10.10–10.15 MHz must satisfy **both** provisions simultaneously; the binding number is the lower one, i.e. **200 W PEP**. Outside that segment, absent another specific provision, the binding number is **1.5 kW PEP**.
- On top of whichever numeric ceiling applies, § 97.313(a) independently requires that the station use only the **minimum transmitter power necessary** to carry out the desired communications. Compliance with 1.5 kW or 200 W is a ceiling, not an entitlement; operating at the ceiling when less power suffices is itself non-compliant with (a).
- The quoted text of (c)(1) contains **no geographic or condition qualifier** — it is a flat segment-wide cap, unlike provisions elsewhere in Part 97 that are region-dependent.

## 4. Measure and unit conventions

- **Unit:** the general limit is expressed in the rule in **kW**; the segment limit in **W**. This answer preserves the rule's own units (1.5 kW; 200 W) and additionally gives the converted form (1.5 kW = 1500 W) so the two can be compared without unit error.
- **Measure:** both limits are expressed in the rule as **PEP (peak envelope power)**. Mean power, average power, and carrier power are *not* the measures named in § 97.313 and must not be substituted when testing compliance or when reporting these figures.
- **Drafting nuance (worth noting, does not change the numbers):** § 97.313(b) says "transmitter power" while § 97.313(c) says "transmitter power output". Both clauses nevertheless attach the qualifier "PEP", and both figures are therefore reported here as PEP.

## 5. Stated caveat on the PEP definition

The *definition* of peak envelope power (and of "transmitter power") lives in the Part 97 definitions section, **§ 97.3**, not in § 97.313. # Compliance memo — 40 CFR § 50.19, 8-hour primary ozone NAAQS: level and attainment criterion

## 0. Scope, version pinning, and confidence labels

**Version applied:** the currently codified text of 40 CFR § 50.19 — the **2015** 8-hour ozone NAAQS (0.070 ppm) — not the 2008 revision (0.075 ppm). This is the version that governs current design values, current designations, and current State Implementation Plan (SIP) / permit analyses. If a reader's purpose is a historical compliance period (e.g., a 2009–2011 design value judged against the 2008 standard), the answer changes; see § 5.

Every statement below carries one of three labels:

| Label | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **V** | Verified against the eCFR material retrieved for this task (the 2015 8-hour primary and secondary ozone NAAQS codified at 40 CFR 50.19; level 0.070 ppm; the 3-year-average-of-fourth-highest criterion; Appendix U as the ozone attainment-calculation appendix). |
| **R** | Recalled from domain knowledge; consistent with **V** but **not** re-verified from primary text in this session. Confirm before use in a filing, designation recommendation, or enforcement document. |
| **U** | Unverified; flag as an open item. |

**Explicit non-scope:** no site-specific data, no design-value computation for a named monitor, and no attainment designation is performed here. This is regulatory-text interpretation plus the arithmetic rule that applies it.

---

## 1. Ask 1 — the level of the standard

**Answer: 0.070 ppm** (parts per million by volume), for both the **primary** (health-based) and **secondary** (welfare-based) 8-hour ozone NAAQS. **[V]**

| Attribute | Value |
|---|---|
| Numeric level | **0.070 ppm** = 7.0 × 10⁻² ppm |
| Equivalent in ppb | **70 ppb** (× 1000) |
| Approximate mass concentration (informational only, 25 °C, 1 atm, 1 ppb O3 ≈ 1.96 µg/m³) | ≈ **137 µg/m³** (70 × 1.96 = 137.2) |
| Codified unit | **ppm** — the regulation states the level in ppm; ppb and µg/m³ are conversions, not the codified form |
| Precision as codified | three decimal places (0.001 ppm granularity) |
| Primary vs. secondary | **Identical level** — § 50.19 codifies the 2015 8-hour primary *and* secondary ozone NAAQS at 0.070 ppm; the two differ in purpose (health vs. public welfare/vegetation), not in level or form for ozone. **[V]** |
| Averaging basis | daily maximum 8-hour average concentrations (not 1-hour, not annual mean) |

**Do not report** 0.075 ppm (2008) or 0.08 ppm (1997) as the current level, and do not report the 1-hour 0.12 ppm standard (1979) as if it were the 8-hour standard. See § 5.

---

## 2. Ask 2 — when the standard is met at a monitoring site

**Verdict identifier (the answer of record):**

```
O3_8HR_PRIMARY_MET_WHEN_3YR_AVG_4TH_HIGHEST_8HR_MAX_LE_0.070_PPM
```

**Expanded in words:** the 2015 8-hour primary ozone NAAQS is **met** at a monitoring site when the **3-year average of the annual fourth-highest daily maximum 8-hour average ozone concentrations** is **less than or equal to 0.070 ppm**. **[V]**

### 2.1 The test, step by step

1. **Hourly data → 8-hour averages.** From valid hourly ozone concentrations, compute running 8-hour averages for the day (the specific set of 8-hour periods and the validity rule are stated in 40 CFR Part 50 **Appendix U** — see § 6 for the recall-status flag).
2. **Daily maximum 8-hour average.** For each day, take the higest of that day's 8-hour averages. One value per day.
3. **Annual fourth-highest.** Within one ozone season/year, rank the valid daily maxima and take the **4th higest**. This — not the single peak — is the year's statistic. (The 4th-highest, rather than the 1st, is the deliberate design choice that keeps a single exceptional day from driving the metric.)
4. **Three-year average.** Average the fourth-highest values from **three consecutive years** (arithmetic mean of three numbers).
5. **Rounding.** Round the 3-year average to **three decimal places (nearest 0.001 ppm)** before comparison. **[R]** — this rounding convention is part of the codified scheme and of EPA's design-value practice; confirm the exact wording in Appendix U before relying on a borderline case.
6. **Comparison.** Compare the rounded 3-year average (the **design value**, DV) with 0.070 ppm:
   - **DV ≤ 0.070 ppm → the site meets the standard.**
   - **DV ≥ 0.071 ppm → the site does not meet the standard** (it is a violating site).
7. **Site vs. area.** The comparison in step 6 is a **site-level** determination. **Attainment** is an **area-level** designation informed by the design values at the monitors in the area; a site-level exceedance is the trigger for the area-level analysis, not itself a designation.

### 2.2 Worked example (self-consistency demonstration)

| Year 1 4th-highest | Year 2 4th-highest | Year 3 4th-highest | 3-yr mean (raw) | Rounded to 0.001 | Verdict vs. 0.070 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.068 | 0.071 | 0.069 | 0.06933… | 0.069 | **MET** |
| 0.070 | 0.070 | 0.070 | 0.07000 | 0.070 | **MET** (equality meets — "less than or equal to") |
| 0.072 | 0.069 | 0.070 | 0.07033… | 0.070 | **MET** |
| 0.071 | 0.070 | 0.071 | 0.07066… | 0.071 | **NOT MET** |
| 0.074 | 0.073 | 0.075 | 0.07400 | 0.074 | **NOT MET** (would have met the 2008 0.075 standard) |
| 0.0704 (single-year edge) | — | — | 0.0704 (illustrative) | 0.070 | **MET** |
| 0.0705 (single-year edge) | — | — | 0.0705 (illustrative) | 0.071 | **NOT MET** |

Every "MET" row rounds to ≤ 0.070; every "NOT MET" row rounds to ≥ 0.071. No example contradicts the 0.070 ppm threshold stated in § 1.

---

## 3. Common compliance traps

| Trap | Correct treatment |
|---|---|
| Using the **highest** daily max instead of the **4th-highest** | Overstates violations; the form is the 4th-highest. |
| Using **one year** instead of a **3-year average** | A single bad year does not by itself establish a violation. |
| Comparing **before rounding** or rounding to 2 decimals | Round to 0.001 ppm (three decimals) under the current scheme. **[R]** |
| Treating a **1-hour** or **annual-mean** metric as the 8-hour standard | Different form; not the § 50.19 standard. |
| Using data from a **non-reference/non-equivalent** method | Only data from a reference or designated-equivalent method count (Appendix I to Part 50). **[R]** |
| Ignoring **data completeness** | A 4th-highest value requires a valid year of data (Appendix U; Part 58). An incomplete year cannot produce a valid design value. **[R]** — see § 6. |
| Ignoring **exceptional events** | Data influenced by excepted events (wildfires, stratospheric ozone intrusion, etc.) may be excluded only under the exceptional-events provision (40 CFR § 50.14) with the required concurrence. **[R]** |
| Treating **primary and secondary** as different levels | For ozone they are the same level and form; they differ only in the welfare/health basis. |

---

## 4. What this means operationally (brief)

- A site with a current design value of **0.070 ppm or below is in compliance** with the 8-hour primary ozone NAAQS; **0.071 ppm or above is a violation** of the site-level test.
- Compliance is assessed on a **rolling 3-year window**; a site can move into or out of compliance as years roll off.
- The **level alone is not the whole test** — the form (4th-highest, 3-year mean, 3-decimal rounding) and the supporting appendices (Appendix U for calculation; Appendix I for method; Part 58 for monitoring/season) are part of the codified scheme. **[V/R as labelled]**

---

## 5. Version dependence — regulatory history

| Revision | Pollutant/metric | Level | Status for this answer |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1979 | Photochemical oxidants, 1-hour | 0.12 ppm | Historical; superseded **[R]** |
| 1997 | Ozone, 8-hour, 4th-highest, 3-year mean | 0.08 ppm | Historical; superseded **[R]** |
| 2008 | Ozone, 8-hour, 4th-highest, 3-year mean | 0.075 ppm | Historical; superseded — **not** the answer **[V]** |
| **2015 (current)** | **Ozone, 8-hour, 4th-highest, 3-year mean** | **0.070 ppm** | **The answer [V]** |

**Notes on the transition:** the 2008 revision's 0.075 ppm does not match the level in the current § 50.19 text, which is why the question must be read as targeting the 2015 revision in force now. **[V]** A precise historical effective-date citation for the 2008→2015 transition was **not recovered** in this session; I recall publication on 26 October 2015 (80 FR 65292) with an effective date of 28 December 2015, and for 2008 publication on 27 March 2008 (73 FR 16436) with an effective date of 27 May 2008 — both **[U]**. Do not put these dates in a filing without checking the Federal Register.

**Historical rounding caveat [U]:** the 1997 8-hour standard is widely understood to have been implemented with rounding of the 3-year average to two decimal places, which effectively permitted design values up to 0.084 ppm; the 2008 rule changed the rounding to three decimal places. This is background only and does not affect the current answer, but verify it before using the 1997 standard in a historical analysis.

**Pending/proposed changes [U]:** the 2015 standard has been the subject of policy review and litigated; no codified change to 0.070 ppm was retrieved here. Treat 0.070 ppm as the operative level and check the current eCFR text for any amendment before relying on it.

---

## 6. Verification status — what to confirm before relying on this

| Item | Status | How to close |
|---|---|---|
| 2015 8-hour primary and secondary ozone NAAQS codified at § 50.19; level 0.070 ppm | **V** | — |
| Met when the 3-year average of the annual 4th-highest daily max 8-hour average is ≤ 0.070 ppm | **V** | — |
| Appendix U is the ozone attainment-calculation appendix | **V** | — |
| Exact paragraph lettering/quotable text within § 50.19 | **R** | Pull the eCFR text of § 50.19 and quote verbatim for any filing. |
| Rounding of the 3-year average to three decimal places | **R** | Confirm wording in Appendix U. |
| Data-completeness percentages (the widely used 75 % hourly / 75 % of days conventions) and the exact set of 8-hour periods used for the daily max | **R** | Do **not** rely on these from this memo; read Appendix U § 2–3 directly. |
| Exceptional-events exclusion (§ 50.14) mechanics | **R** | Read § 50.14 and the applicable administrator's concurrence procedure. |
| Ozone monitoring season per state (Part 58) | **R** | Confirm the state's approved season; it bounds which days can produce valid daily maxima. |
| Federal Register citation numbers and effective dates | **U** | Verify in the Federal Register. |

---

## 7. Self-consistency check (the numbers in this memo against the threshold it sets)

- Threshold set and used throughout: **0.070 ppm**.
- Rounding unit: **0.001 ppm**; comparison performed on the rounded 3-year mean.
- Every example labelled MET rounds to 0.068–0.070 → **≤ 0.070** ✓
- Every example labelled NOT MET rounds to 0.071–0.075 → **> 0.070** ✓
- 0.0704 → 0.070 (MET) and 0.0705 → 0.071 (NOT MET) straddle the threshold without crossing it ✓
- 0.070 ppm = 70 ppb (× 1000) ✓; ≈ 137 µg/m³ at 1.96 µg/m³ per ppb → 70 × 1.96 = 137.2 ✓ (approximate, informasional)
- Historical levels 0.12 > 0.08 > 0.075 > 0.070 ppm — monotone tightening, and none is presented as current ✓

---

## 8. Bottom line

**Level:** 0.070 ppm (70 ppb), 8-hour primary ozone NAAQS, 2015 revision, codified at 40 CFR § 50.19; the secondary standard is at the same level. **[V]**

**Met when:** at a monitoring site, the 3-year average of the annual fourth-highest daily maximum 8-hour average ozone concentration — rounded to three decimal places — is **less than or equal to 0.070 ppm**. **[V]**

**Not met when:** that design value is **0.071 ppm or higher**. **[V]**

# NIST SP 800-63B-4 — Password Length Requirements

Source of record: **NIST SP 800-63B-4, Digital Identity Guidelines: Authentication and Authenticator Management, final revision (published 31 July 2025)**. Not the initial or second public draft — the draft figures differ and are the most common way this question is answered incorrectly.

## 1. Answers

| # | Question | Answer | Normative force |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Minimum length verifiers must require when the password is the **sole** authentication factor | **15 characters** | SHALL — mandatory |
| 2 | Minimum length when the password is used **only as one factor within MFA** | **8 characters** | SHALL — mandatory |
| 3 | Maximum length verifiers should permit **at least** | **64 characters** | SHOULD — recommendation |

## 2. How to read each requirement (direction of comparison)

**Asks 1 and 2 — floors.** These are minimums the verifier must *accept*. A verifier that rejects a 15-character password presented as the only factor is non-conforming. A verifier that rejects an 8-character password presented alongside a second factor is non-conforming. The requirement is conditioned on **use case, not on AAL**: the same verifier may hold both rules and apply whichever matches how the password is being used. In practice the 15-character rule governs AAL1-style single-factor password authentication (a password alone is only a permitted single-factor authenticator at the lowest assurance level), while the 8-character rule governs AAL2/AAL3 configurations where the password is one of several factors.

**Ask 3 — a floor on the cap, not a cap.** The recommendation is that verifiers and CSPs should *permit* a maximum password length of at least 64 characters. The 64 is the smallest acceptable upper bound, not a limit to enforce. Concretely:
- Rejecting a 64-character password purely for length is a violation of the recommendation.
- Setting the enforced cap at 128, 256, or no cap at all is fully compliant and preferred.
- Setting the cap at exactly 64 is compliant: 64 characters are permitted, so the "at least 64" condition is met, and a 65-character password may then be rejected.
- Reading 64 as "passwords must be no longer than 64" inverts the requirement.

## 3. Failure modes this answer is written to prevent

1. **Applying the 8-character minimum to single-factor use.** 8 is valid only when a second, independent factor is actually enforced. If MFA is optional, configurable off, or bypassable, the effective policy is single-factor and 15 applies.
2. **Quoting a draft value.** Earlier public drafts of SP 800-63B-4 carried different figures. Confirm the policy cites the final revision, and record the revision date in the policy document so the citation is auditable.
3. **Truncation.** A 64-character permitted maximum is meaningless if the verifier silently truncates to 20 characters before hashing or comparison. Verification must consume the entire password. Length policy and truncation behavior must be reviewed together.
4. **Confusing SHOULD with SHALL.** 15 and 8 are mandatory; 64 is a recommendation. A conformance report should not present all three at the same normative weight.
5. **Capping below the stated minimum.** No configuration should ever have `max_length < min_length`; with these figures the cap must be ≥64, which is comfortably above both floors.

## 4. Reference policy configuration

```yaml
password_policy:
  source: "NIST SP 800-63B-4 (final, 2025-07-31)"
  min_length_single_factor: 15     # SHALL
  min_length_mfa_component: 8      # SHALL
  max_length_floor: 64             # SHOULD permit at least this many
  max_length_enforced: 128         # >= 64; prefer 128+ or unbounded
  truncation: none                 # verify the full password
  character_set: unrestricted      # accept Unicode and all printable chars incl. space
  trim_whitespace: false           # do not strip leading/trailing spaces
  composition_rules: none          # no forced mix of character classes
  periodic_rotation: none          # no forced expiry
  breach_screening: required       # block known-compromised passwords
```

Selection rule at authentication time:

```
required_min = (password_is_only_factor) ? 15 : 8
if len(password) < required_min: reject
effective_max  = max(max_length_enforced, 64)   # never below 64
if len(password) > effective_max: reject
verify_full(password)                            # no truncation
```

Note on `required_min`: if a deployment cannot reliably determine at runtime whether a second factor is enforced for a given account, use 15 for all accounts. 15 satisfies both rules and removes the bypass risk in failure mode 1.

## 5. Conformance test cases

| Input | Context | Expected |
|---|---|---|
| 14 chars | single-factor | reject (below 15) |
| 15 chars | single-factor | accept |
| 7 chars | with second factor enforced | reject (below 8) |
| 8 chars | with second factor enforced | accept |
| 8 chars | single-factor / MFA bypassable | reject |
| 63 chars | any | accept |
| 64 chars | any | accept |
| 65 chars | any | accept if cap > 64; rejection allowed only if cap is exactly 64 |
| 200 chars, mixed Unicode | any | accept, unmodified, no truncation |
| password with leading/trailing spaces | any | accept, spaces preserved |

## 6. Scope and grounding caveats

- The three figures are taken from the project's researched-facts block, which cites the final SP 800-63B-4 publication and explicitly distinguishes it from the drafts. The password requirements sit in the authenticator-requirements section of SP 800-63B-4 (the passwords subsection, §3.1.1.2 in the -4 numbering); the exact section number and verbatim wording should be confirmed against the published PDF before the figures are quoted in a formal compliance artifact, since subsection numbering shifted across revisions.
- The wording above is paraphrase, not verbatim quotation. Where a contract or audit requires exact language, quote from the published PDF rather than from this document.
- Out of scope here: composition rules, rotation, breach-list screening, rate limiting, and salt/hashing requirements. They are noted only where they interact with length (truncation, screening) and are not answered by this document.
- These requirements are not conditioned on AAL as reported; they are conditioned on whether the password is the sole factor or an MFA component.
