## 1. Answers (general rule, 49 CFR 395.3(a), property-carrying CMV)

| # | Question | Answer | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Consecutive hours off duty required before driving | **10 consecutive hours off duty** | 49 CFR 395.3(a)(1) |
| 2 | Consecutive hours after which the driver may no longer drive | **14 consecutive hours** (measured from coming on duty after 10 consecutive hours off duty) | 49 CFR 395.3(a)(2) |
| 3 | Total hours that may be driven within that period | **11 cumulative hours of driving** | 49 CFR 395.3(a)(3) |

The three figures are independent conditions, not one budget. A driver satisfies all three only if every one of them is met; the binding constraint on any given day is whichever is hit first.

## 2. Governing text and how each figure operates

Section 395.3(a) opens with "Except as otherwise provided in § 395.1," so these are the default limits that apply unless a § 395.1 exception is actually established for the driver (see § 5 below).

**(a)(1) — Off-duty reset: 10 consecutive hours.** A driver may not drive until 10 consecutive hours off duty have been completed. Off-duty and sleeper-berth time both count toward the 10; on-duty-not-driving time does not. This is a precondition to the workday, not a component of it.

**(a)(2) — The 14-hour window.** After coming on duty following 10 consecutive hours off duty, the driver may not drive after the 14th consecutive hour. Two points that are routinely misread:
- The 14 hours is **elapsed clock time**, not accumulated on-duty time. Off-duty time taken inside the window does **not** extend it (the only mechanism that can pause it is the sleeper-berth provision at § 395.1(g)). So the answer to the question as phrased — "after how many consecutive hours on duty" — is 14 consecutive elapsed hours, counted from the moment the driver comes on duty.
- The window covers all driving plus all on-duty-not-driving time; it is not a 14-hour driving allowance.

**(a)(2) interruption rule (subparagraph (ii) of the current codified text).** Driving is not permitted if more than 8 cumulative hours of driving time have passed without at least one consecutive 30-minute interruption in driving status. The interruption may be satisfied by off-duty, sleeper-berth, on-duty-not-driving time, or any combination of the three. Drivers qualifying for the short-haul exceptions in § 395.1(e)(1) or (2) are excepted from this interruption rule only.

**(a)(3) — 11-hour driving limit.** No more than 11 cumulative hours of driving within the window. Driving time is time behind the wheel in a CMV as recorded under § 395.8 (paper/electronic RODS) or § 395.15 (automatic on-board recorder).

Ordering check: 8 (interruption trigger) < 11 (driving cap) < 14 (window). The driving cap is contained inside the window, as it must be.

## 3. Counting conventions (needed to apply the numbers correctly)

| Term | What counts | Source |
|---|---|---|
| "Off duty" for the 10-hour reset | Off-duty + sleeper-berth time; must be consecutive and uninterrupted except as § 395.1(g) permits | § 395.2; § 395.1(g) |
| "On duty" for the 14-hour window | All driving time + all on-duty-not-driving time; window starts at the first on-duty or driving minute after the reset | § 395.2; § 395.3(a)(2) |
| "Driving time" for the 11-hour limit | Time actually operating a CMV in commerce, per RODS | § 395.2; § 395.8; § 395.15 |

Sleeper-berth note: § 395.1(g) allows the 10-hour requirement to be met by a pairing of at least 8 consecutive sleeper-berth hours plus a separate period of at least 2 hours (off-duty, sleeper berth, or a combination), and the two qualifying periods exclude the 14-hour window from the calculation. That is a recalculating mechanism, not a reduction of the 10/11/14 figures — the figures themselves are unchanged.

Separate limits that must not be confused with these three: the 60-hour/7-day and 70-hour/8-day on-duty limits in § 395.3(b), and the 34-hour restart in § 395.3(c). A driver can be fully compliant with 10/11/14 and still be in violation of (b).

## 4. Worked example (log-level check)

Driver completes 10 consecutive hours off duty at 06:00 Monday.

| Clock | Status | Cumulative driving | Hours into 14-hour window | Driving permitted? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 06:00 | On duty (pre-trip) | 0.0 | 0 | Yes |
| 06:30–11:30 | Driving | 5.0 | 5.5 | Yes |
| 11:30–12:00 | On duty not driving (fuel, scale) | 5.0 | 6.0 | Yes — this 30 min also satisfies the interruption rule |
| 12:00–17:00 | Driving | 10.0 | 11.0 | Yes |
| 17:00–17:30 | Off duty | 10.0 | 11.5 | Yes — off-duty time does not pause the window |
| 17:30–18:30 | Driving | 11.0 | 12.5 | Yes — 11th hour reached at 18:30 |
| 18:30–20:00 | On duty not driving | 11.0 | 14.0 | **No** — 11-hour driving cap reached, and the 14-hour window closes at 20:00 |

At 20:00 the driver must not drive again until 10 consecutive hours off duty are complete (i.e., not before 06:00 Tuesday), unless a § 395.1 exception applies.

## 5. Scope: what would change these numbers

These figures are the default. They are altered only where a specific § 395.1 provision is actually established for the driver:

| Provision | Effect on the three figures |
|---|---|
| Short-haul, § 395.1(e)(1)/(2) | Does **not** change 10/11/14. Exempts the driver from the 30-minute interruption rule only (and from RODS under § 395.8). |
| Adverse driving conditions, § 395.1(b)(1) | Driver may drive "not more than two additional hours beyond the maximum allowable hours permitted under § 395.3(a)" to complete the run or reach a place of safety. FMCSA guidance treats this as extending both the 11-hour driving limit and the 14-hour window by up to 2 hours. It is a completion/safety provision, not a general extension of the duty day. |
| Sleeper berth, § 395.1(g) | Does not change 10/11/14; changes how the 14-hour window is computed across a qualifying 8/2 pairing. |
| Oilfield / other § 395.1 specialty operations | Different limits may apply; the general 10/11/14 figures would not be the controlling ones. |

If the driver in question is under a short-haul or adverse-driving posture, only the interruption rule or the outer boundary shifts — the three headline values (10, 14, 11) remain the baseline against which any extension is measured.

## 6. Machine-checkable specification

For a compliance system or ELD rule engine, encode the general rule as:

```
RESET_OFF_DUTY_HOURS      = 10.0   # consecutive; off-duty + sleeper berth
MAX_WINDOW_HOURS          = 14.0   # consecutive elapsed from first on-duty after reset
MAX_DRIVING_HOURS         = 11.0   # cumulative within the window
INTERRUPTION_DRIVING_HRS  = 8.0    # cumulative driving before a break is required
INTERRUPTION_LENGTH_MIN   = 30     # consecutive; off-duty, sleeper, or on-duty-not-driving

function can_drive(now, window_start, driving_in_window, last_interruption_end):
    if hours_since_reset_end(now) < RESET_OFF_DUTY_HOURS: return DENY("395.3(a)(1)")
    if hours_since(window_start) >= MAX_WINDOW_HOURS:   return DENY("395.3(a)(2)")

       and not interruption_met(now, INTERRUPTION_LENGTH_MIN):
        return DENY("395.3(a)(2)(ii)")
    return ALLOW
```

Invariant the engine must enforce: `MAX_DRIVING_HOURS <= MAX_WINDOW_HOURS` (11 <= 14). Any configured exception (e.g., +2 hours adverse driving) must be applied to both the driving limit and the window together, preserving that ordering.

ANSWER — 47 CFR § 97.313 (Transmitter power standards)

| # | Question | Value | Unit | Measure | Rule cite |
|---|----------|-------|------|---------|-----------|
| 1 | General maximum transmitter power for an amateur station | 1.5 | kW | PEP (peak envelope power) | 47 CFR § 97.313(b) |
| 2 | Limit applicable on the 10.10–10.15 MHz segment (the lower / more restrictive cap) | 200 | W | PEP (peak envelope power) | 47 CFR § 97.313(c)(1) |

Equivalently: 1,500 W PEP general; 200 W PEP on 10.10–10.15 MHz (30 m).

1. GENERAL MAXIMUM — 1.5 kW PEP (1,500 watts peak envelope power)
Source text, § 97.313(b): "No station may transmit with a transmitter power exceeding 1.5 kW PEP."
This is the general ceiling applicable absent a more restrictive band, segment, or emission limitation. It is a ceiling, not an entitlement: a station must still comply with every more restrictive limit that applies to the frequency, emission type, or location in use.

2. 10.10–10.15 MHz SEGMENT — 200 W PEP
Source text, § 97.313(c), opening and (c)(1): "No station may transmit with a transmitter power output exceeding 200 W PEP: (1) On the 10.10-10.15 MHz segment;"
The word "lower" in the question is read as "the lower (more restrictive) maximum," i.e. 200 W PEP, not as a minimum-power floor. For clarity: § 97.313 contains no minimum-power floor stated in watts; the only minimum-related obligation is the qualitative duty in § 97.313(a) to use the minimum power necessary (see § 4 below).

3. UNIT AND MEASURE — what to state with each figure
- Unit: watts (W) or kilowatts (kW) — a power unit, not field strength, not dBW, not ERP/EIRP.
- Measure: PEP — peak envelope power, the average power supplied to the antenna transmission line by a transmitter during one RF cycle at the crest of the modulation envelope under normal operating conditions (the PEP definition appears in the § 97.3 definitions paragraph; confirm the exact subparagraph letter/number against the current eCFR before quoting it in a filing — I did not verify that subparagraph designation).
- Consequence of the PEP measure: 1.5 kW PEP is not 1.5 kW average/continuous. For a linearly amplified SSB signal the average power is materially below the PEP figure; for CW the two are close. A peak-reading wattmeter, or average power corrected for duty factor, is the usual bench method; the rule prescribes the quantity, not the instrument.
- Textual nuance worth flagging: § 97.313(b) says "transmitter power" while § 97.313(c) says "transmitter power output." The numeric limits and their PEP measure are unaffected; only a precise quotation should preserve the wording as written.

4. COMPANION PROVISION — § 97.313(a)
"An amateur station must use the minimum transmitter power necessary to carry out the desired communications." This is a duty of the licensee and coexists with the numeric caps; it is not a numeric limit and is not an answer to ask 1 or 2.

5. ARITHMETIC / CONSISTENCY CHECK
- 1.5 kW = 1,500 W PEP; 200 W PEP = 0.2 kW PEP.
- 200 W < 1,500 W, so the segment limit is properly the lower (more restrictive) of the two: check passes.
- Ratio 1500/200 = 7.5; 10·log10(7.5) = 8.75 dB. The 10.10–10.15 MHz cap is 8.75 dB below the general cap. Consistent with both stated values; no stated threshold is violated by any figure in this deliverable.

- Governing code: 47 CFR Part 97, Subpart D (Technical Standards), § 97.313.

- This is regulatory information, not legal advice.

Ask 3 ("give each with its unit and measure") is a formatting requirement, satisfied by the table in § 1 above; it is not a value or verdict and therefore carries no separate results entry. The two value asks are reported as 1.5 kW PEP and 200 W PEP.

COMPLIANCE MEMO — 29 CFR § 1926.501(b)(1), UNPROTECTED SIDES AND EDGES

1. QUESTION PRESENTED
At what height above a lower level must an employee on a walking/working surface with an unprotected side or edge be protected from falling under 29 CFR § 1926.501(b)(1), and by which systems?

2. ANSWER
(1) Threshold: 6 feet (1.8 m) or more above a lower level. The duty attaches at 6 ft — the standard reads '6 feet (1.8 m) or more,' so a surface exactly 6 ft above the lower level is already covered; there is no tolerance band and no rounding allowance. Below 6 ft, (b)(1) does not itself require fall protection (other hazards or standards may still apply).
(2) Systems: the employee 'shall be protected from falling by the use of' (a) guardrail systems, (b) safety net systems, or (c) personal fall arrest systems. These three, and only these three, are the means of compliance named in (b)(1).

3. CONTROLLING TEXT (verbatim)
29 CFR § 1926.501(b)(1) — 'Unprotected sides and edges.'
"Each employee on a walking/working surface (horizontal and vertical surface) with an unprotected side or edge which is 6 feet (1.8 m) or more above a lower level shall be protected from falling by the use of guardrail systems, safety net systems, or personal fall arrest systems."
Source: eCFR, 29 CFR Part 1926, Subpart M, § 1926.501 (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-XVII/part-1926/subpart-M/section-1926.501); corroborated by OSHA's published standard page (https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1926/1926.501) and the GovInfo CFR XML for 29 CFR 1926.501. Cite the section as in force on the date of the compliance determination; the quoted language has been stable across recent annual CFR editions.

4. HOW THE HEIGHT IS MEASURED
- Measured vertically from the walking/working surface on which the employee stands to the lower level to which the employee could fall — not along a slope, not to the top of a guardrail, not to the employee's feet versus head.
- 'Walking/working surface' expressly includes both horizontal and vertical surfaces (per the parenthetical in (b)(1)); the same 6 ft (1.8 m) trigger governs vertical surfaces.
- 'Lower level' is defined in § 1926.500(b): 'those areas or surfaces to which an employee can fall,' including ground level, floors, platforms, ramps, excavations, pits, tanks, material, water, equipment, structures, or portions thereof.
- 'Unprotected side or edge' is defined in § 1926.500(b) as any side or edge (except at entrances to points of access) of a walking/working surface — e.g., floor, roof, ramp, or runway — where there is no wall or guardrail system at least 39 inches (1.0 m) high. A compliant wall or 39-in guardrail therefore removes the edge from (b)(1) exposure; anything less does not.

5. WHAT 'PROTECTED BY' REQUIRES — SYSTEM CRITERIA
Naming a system is not enough; the installed system must meet the corresponding criteria in § 1926.502:
- Guardrail systems → § 1926.502(b) (top rail 42 in ±3 in, midrail, 200 lb load, toe boards where required, etc.).
- Safety net systems → § 1926.502(c) (installation as close as practicable under the surface, drop-test/ certification, mesh, border rope, clearance, etc.).
- Personal fall arrest systems → § 1926.502(d) (full-body harness, attachment to anchorage, anchorage strength 5,000 lb or engineered, free-fall limits, deceleration distance, prompt rescue, no lifeline/ lanyard tie-off to incompatible points, etc.).
A compliance finding should record the specific § 1926.502 paragraph the chosen system satisfies, together with the field verification of that criterion.

6. LIMITS OF THIS ANSWER (state these in the file)
- Scoped to § 1926.501(b)(1) only. Other paragraphs of § 1926.501 set their own duties and, in some cases, their own 6 ft (1.8 m) trigger and their own permitted systems (e.g., holes, hoist areas, ramps, excavation edges, leading edges). If the exposure is also described by another paragraph, that paragraph must be checked separately.
- (b)(1) does not reference the fall protection plan option of § 1926.502(k). A fall protection plan is therefore not a substitute for the three named systems under (b)(1) itself; that option appears in other provisions (e.g., leading edge work, precast concrete erection, residential construction). Do not list it as a (b)(1) compliance route.
- Warning line systems, safety monitoring systems, positioning device systems, and designated areas are also not named in (b)(1); they appear in other Subpart M provisions (e.g., roofing work at low slopes) and must not be presented as satisfying (b)(1).
- Residential construction is not treated differently in the text of (b)(1); if the work is residential, confirm the applicable paragraph and any directive guidance separately rather than assuming an exemption.
- Subpart M does not apply to the equipment and operations excluded by § 1926.500(a)(2) (e.g., scaffolds, stairways and ladders, and certain other operations governed by their own subparts); confirm scope before applying (b)(1).
- OSHA-approved State Plans must be at least as effective as the federal standard and may be stricter or have different numeric triggers; if the worksite is in a State Plan jurisdiction, verify the State's own text.

7. VERIFICATION TRAIL
Answer rests on the verbatim text of § 1926.501(b)(1) as published on eCFR (fetched 2026-11-15, sha256 3e4c6b147793), corroborated by the OSHA standard page and the GovInfo CFR XML for 29 CFR 1926.501. Re-pull the eCFR text on the date of use to confirm no amendment has intervened; record the retrieval date in the compliance file.

# Ozone NAAQS under 40 CFR § 50.19 — level of the primary 8-hour standard and the site-level test for meeting it

## 0. Controlling text (current eCFR, verbatim)

> § 50.19 — National primary and secondary ambient air quality standards for ozone
>
> (a) The level of the national 8-hour primary ambient air quality standard for ozone (O3) is 0.070 parts per million (ppm), daily maximum 8-hour average, measured by a reference method based on appendix D to this part and designated in accordance with part 53 of this chapter or an equivalent method designated in accordance with part 53 of this chapter.
>
> (b) The 8-hour primary O3 ambient air quality standard is met at an ambient air quality monitoring site when the 3-year average of the annual fourth-highest daily maximum 8-hour average O3 concentration is less than or equal to 0.070 ppm, as determined in accordance with appendix U to this part.

Source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-40/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-50/section-50.19 (retrieved 2026-11-15T09:48:52Z, sha256 29cc1e46ed44).

## 1. Level of the national 8-hour primary standard (ask 1)

**0.070 ppm** — equivalently 70 ppb — expressed as a **daily maximum 8-hour average**.

What that level is and is not:

- It is a concentration metric, not an annual mean, not a seasonal mean, and not a 1-hour value.
- The regulated metric is the *daily maximum 8-hour average*: for each day, the highest of that day's 8-hour running averages of the hourly ozone concentrations.
- The regulation is written in ppm to three decimal places; one unit in the third decimal place equals 1 ppb (0.001 ppm = 1 ppb). State the level as 0.070 ppm in any regulatory document and, if a ppb rendering is used for readability, render it as 70 ppb — do not mix the two within one table.
- It is a *primary* (public-health) standard. The excerpt retrieved covers only paragraphs (a) and (b). Do not copy these numbers onto the secondary (welfare) standard without reading the section's remaining paragraphs directly.

## 2. When the standard is met at a monitoring site (ask 2)

A site meets the 8-hour primary ozone standard **if and only if**

```
round3( [ A(Y1) + A(Y2) + A(Y3) ] / 3 )  <=  0.070 ppm
```

where A(Y) is the **annual fourth-highest daily maximum 8-hour average** ozone concentration for year Y, and Y1–Y3 are three consecutive years. Determination is made in accordance with **Appendix U to 40 CFR Part 50**.

Two boundary points that decide real cases:

- The test is **≤**, not <. A design value of exactly 0.070 ppm (70 ppb) **meets** the standard.
- A design value of 0.071 ppm (71 ppb) **does not** meet it. There is no rounding tolerance beyond the single round3 step in § 3.

## 3. Computation procedure (reproducible, step by step)

1. **Data.** Collect valid hourly ozone concentrations from a monitor operating a reference method (Appendix D to Part 50) or an equivalent method (Part 53), for the required ozone monitoring season defined for the area in Appendix D to Part 50, for three consecutive years.
2. **8-hour averages.** For each hour, compute the 8-hour average as the mean of that hour and the preceding 7 hours. An 8-hour average is valid only if at least 75% of its 8 hourly values are present (≥ 6 of 8).
3. **Daily maximum.** For each day, take the highest of that day's 8-hour averages. A daily maximum is valid only if at least 75% of the day's 8-hour averages are valid (≥ 18 of 24).
4. **Exceptional events.** Remove data only under 40 CFR § 50.14 (exceptional events) and only after the required concurrence; do not drop high days for any other reason.
5. **Annual fourth-highest.** For each year, sort that year's valid daily maxima in descending order and take the 4th value: A(Y1), A(Y2), A(Y3).
6. **Design value.** Average the three annual fourth-highest values and round to three decimal places (thousandths of ppm), half-up (0.0005 rounds up). This rounded value is the site's ozone design value.
7. **Decision.** Met if the rounded design value ≤ 0.070 ppm; not met if ≥ 0.071 ppm.

Reference implementation (language-agnostic; use decimal arithmetic, not binary floats):

```
from decimal import Decimal, ROUND_HALF_UP

def round3(x):                      # round to thousandths of ppm, half-up
    return Decimal(x).quantize(Decimal('0.001'), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP)

def annual_fourth_max(days):        # days: {date: [24 hourly ppm or None]}
    daily = []
    for hrs in days.values():
        e8 = []
        for h in range(24):         # 8-hr periods ending at each hour of the day
            window = [hrs[(h - k) % 24] for k in range(8)]
            present = [v for v in window if v is not None]
            if len(present) >= 6:   # 75% of 8 hours
                e8.append(sum(present) / len(present))
        if len(e8) >= 18:           # 75% of 24 8-hr averages
            daily.append(max(e8))
    if len(daily) < 4:
        return None                 # annual 4th-highest not defined
    return sorted(daily, reverse=True)[3]

def design_value(y1, y2, y3):
    a = [annual_fourth_max(y) for y in (y1, y2, y3)]
    if any(v is None for v in a):
        return None                 # insufficient data -> no design value
    return round3(sum(a) / 3)

met = design_value(Y1, Y2, Y3) is not None and design_value(Y1, Y2, Y3) <= Decimal('0.070')
```

Note the float trap: `0.0705 * 1000` evaluates to 70.4999… in binary floating point and would round *down* to 0.070, wrongly passing a site that should fail. Use `Decimal` (or integer ppb arithmetic) end to end.

## 4. Rounding convention and worked examples

The single rounding step is the round3 on the 3-year mean, half-up. Truncation is **not** the ozone convention — a mean of 0.0706 truncates to 0.070 (pass) but rounds to 0.071 (fail), and the rounding answer is the correct one.

| Site | A(Y1) | A(Y2) | A(Y3) | Sum (ppm) | Mean (ppm) | Design value | Met? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | 0.072 | 0.069 | 0.071 | 0.212 | 0.0706667 | **0.071** | **No** (> 0.070) |
| B | 0.070 | 0.071 | 0.070 | 0.211 | 0.0703333 | **0.070** | **Yes** (≤ 0.070) |
| C | 0.074 | 0.068 | 0.069 | 0.211 | 0.0703333 | **0.070** | **Yes** (≤ 0.070) |
| D | 0.071 | 0.070 | 0.071 | 0.212 | 0.0706667 | **0.071** | **No** (> 0.070) |

Site C is the case that trips people: a single year at 0.074 ppm does not by itself fail the site, because the form of the standard uses the 4th-highest day of each year and a 3-year average.

Rounding-boundary cases:

| 3-year mean (ppm) | 4th decimal | Design value | Met? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.07049 | 4 | 0.070 | Yes |
| 0.0704 | 4 | 0.070 | Yes |
| 0.0705 | 5 (tie) | 0.071 | No |
| 0.0706 | 6 | 0.071 | No |

**Whole-ppb shortcut (safe when annual fourth-highest values are whole ppb).** The mean of three integer-ppb values is a multiple of 1/3 ppb, so the exact tie at 70.5 ppb is unreachable and the decision reduces to a sum test:

- A(Y1)+A(Y2)+A(Y3) = 210 ppb → 70.000 ppb → 0.070 ppm → **met**
- A(Y1)+A(Y2)+A(Y3) = 211 ppb → 70.333 ppb → 0.070 ppm → **met**
- A(Y1)+A(Y2)+A(Y3) = 212 ppb → 70.667 ppb → 0.071 ppm → **not met**

So, with whole-ppb inputs: **met ⟺ the three annual fourth-highest values sum to 211 ppb or less.** This is exactly equivalent to the ≤ 0.070 ppm statement in § 2 and must not be restated as 212 ppb.

## 5. Data validity and completeness conventions applied in the determination

- 8-hour average validity: ≥ 75% of the 8 hourly values (≥ 6 of 8).
- Daily maximum validity: ≥ 75% of the day's 8-hour averages (≥ 18 of 24).
- Seasonal capture: the annual fourth-highest is only usable when the year's data capture over the required ozone monitoring season meets the completeness requirement in Appendix U; a year that fails it is flagged and the site may have no valid 3-year design value rather than a passing one. Treat missing data as "no design value," never as "meets the standard."
- Exceptional events: exclusion only under 40 CFR § 50.14 with concurrence.

## 6. Measurement basis

§ 50.19(a) requires the measurement to be made by a reference method based on **Appendix D to Part 50** and designated in accordance with **Part 53**, or by an **equivalent method** designated in accordance with Part 53. Data from non-designated sensors may inform operations but cannot establish that the standard is or is not met at a site.

## 7. Scope boundaries — what § 50.19 does not decide

- **Site vs. area.** § 50.19(b) decides whether the standard is met *at a monitoring site*. Whether an *area* is designated attainment/nonattainment is a separate determination under CAA § 107(d) and 40 CFR Part 81, which considers all sites in the area plus other factors. A site result is an input to a designation, not a designation.
- **Multiple monitors at one site.** Where a site carries more than one monitor, apply the test to each monitor's design value and use the highest valid value as the site's result; Appendix U governs any combining of monitors.
- **Primary vs. secondary.** Only the primary standard is answered here. The retrieved excerpt contains paragraphs (a) and (b); read the remaining paragraphs of § 50.19 directly before stating anything about the secondary standard.
- **Date dependence.** The level is version-dependent. The 2015 revision lowered the 8-hour ozone NAAQS to 0.070 ppm and replaced the prior interpretation appendix with Appendix U; earlier versions of the section carried 0.075 ppm (2008) and 0.08 ppm (1997) with a different interpretation appendix. Any document quoting § 50.19 must be date-stamped to the version relied on. The text retrieved on 2026-11-15 shows 0.070 ppm as operative.

## 8. Source-fidelity notes

The level (0.070 ppm) and the met-condition (3-year average of the annual fourth-highest daily maximum 8-hour average ≤ 0.070 ppm, per Appendix U) are taken verbatim from the retrieved § 50.19 text and are the operative answers. The mechanics in § 3–§ 5 above (75% hourly and daily validity thresholds, the half-up rounding at the thousandths place, the exceptional-events carve-out, and the Appendix D seasonal basis) are the conventions Appendix U and Part 50 practice apply; before filing a regulatory submittal, confirm the exact Appendix U wording of the rounding sentence and the completeness percentages against the current appendix text, and confirm the paragraph letters covering the secondary standard in the current § 50.19.

SOURCE: NIST SP 800-63B-4, Digital Identity Guidelines: Authentication and Authenticator Management (final published revision 4). The three figures below come from the password verifier requirements within the passwords section (section 3.1.1.2 'Password Verifier Requirements' in the -4 numbering; the exact number shifts between the IPD and the final, so cite the section title as well as the number when quoting).

ANSWERS

1) Password used as a single-factor authentication mechanism — minimum 15 characters.
   Normative force: SHALL. Verifiers and CSPs SHALL require passwords used as a single-factor authentication mechanism to be a minimum of 15 characters in length. This is a hard requirement, not a recommendation; a verifier that accepts a 12-character single-factor password is non-conformant.

2) Password used only as part of multi-factor authentication — minimum 8 characters.
   Normative force: SHALL (floor), with MAY (permission to go below the single-factor figure). Verifiers and CSPs MAY allow passwords used only as part of MFA to be shorter than the single-factor minimum, but SHALL require them to be a minimum of eight characters. So 8 is the floor, not a target: a verifier is free to require 15 (or more) for MFA passwords as well, but may not go below 8. The 8-character permission is conditional on the password being used only as part of MFA — if the same password authenticator can also be used on its own as a single factor, the 15-character minimum applies, because the lower floor never attaches to a credential that can authenticate alone.

3) Maximum length verifiers should permit at least — 64 characters.
   Normative force: SHOULD. Verifiers and CSPs SHOULD permit a maximum password length of at least 64 characters. Read this as a floor on the upper bound: 64 is the minimum size of the cap a verifier is expected to allow. It is not a ceiling on what a verifier may accept — permitting 128 or 256 characters is conformant and preferred, since it exceeds the recommendation. Setting the cap below 64 (e.g., truncating at 20 or 32) is what the SHOULD is designed to discourage, and doing so also interacts badly with the truncation and character-set requirements in the same section.

COUNTING AND ENCODING CONVENTIONS (needed to apply the numbers correctly)
- All three figures are counted in characters, not bytes. Do not convert 64 characters into a 64-byte buffer; a 64-character password containing multi-byte UTF-8 code points will exceed 64 bytes and must still be accepted end to end (input field, transport, hashing/verifier storage).
- Verifiers are expected to accept Unicode, including spaces, and to normalize consistently (NFKC or NFC, applied identically at enrollment and verification) so that length is measured on a stable representation.
- Length is measured on the password as submitted, not on a truncated or composed form; truncation before hashing effectively lowers the permitted maximum and undercuts the 64-character recommendation.

RELATED REQUIREMENTS IN THE SAME SECTION (context, not asked but they govern how the length rules are implemented)
- Passwords are to be screened against blocklists of commonly used, expected, or compromised values; length minimums do not substitute for screening.
- No composition rules (no mandated mix of upper/lower/digit/symbol) and no periodic rotation without evidence of compromise.
- No composition-based complexity hints; offer guidance rather than rules.
- Rate limiting / throttling of failed attempts, with the associated feedback rules.

VERSION CAVEAT — READ BEFORE APPLYING
SP 800-63B-4 exists in multiple forms (initial public draft, 2nd public draft, final). The single-factor minimum in particular changed across them: earlier drafts used a lower figure (8 characters) for single-factor passwords, and the final revision raises it to 15. The values above are the final-revision values. If your obligation is pinned to a draft (for example a contract or ATO that cites the IPD by date), re-verify against that exact document before adopting 15 — the other two figures (8 for MFA-only, 64 recommended maximum) are stable across these versions, but the single-factor minimum is not. Record the specific publication date/version you are conforming to in your control documentation.

CONFORMANCE CHECK A VERIFIER MUST PASS
- Rejects any single-factor password shorter than 15 characters.
- Rejects any MFA-only password shorter than 8 characters; may reject below 15 if policy chooses to impose the stricter figure uniformly.
- Accepts passwords of at least 64 characters without silent truncation, and counts them in characters across the full path.
- Does not impose composition rules or mandatory rotation.
- Screens new and changed passwords against a blocklist.
